(1) galaxies in low-density environment follow the observed j *–M sequence after major mergers and that (2) the retention factors for the disks are close to unity, whereas those for the bulges are a few times lower.
the j *– M * relation for disks is a result of the secular evolution of galaxies and that it is not a consequence of mergers.
galaxies and their components grow in a quasi–homologous way, with the retention factors of disks being close to unity and those of bulges being a few times smaller.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the angular momentum evolution, kinematical decomposition, and the galaxy–halo connection in a cosmological context.
how the angular momentum of galaxies is inherited from that of their dark matter halos and how the angular momentum distribution is modified by the formation and growth of the galaxies.
the evolution of galactic angular momentum and its relation to the halo angular momentum.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the j *–${M}_{* }$ relation is a natural consequence of galaxy formation and evolution in a hierarchical cosmology.
, in the absence of strong feedback, galaxies and their components are built in a homologous way, while strong feedback may lead to a more heterogeneous assembly.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the angular momentum of the stellar component is conserved in the presence of a strong feedback, while secular evolution is more effective when feedback is weak.
the angular momentum of galaxies is determined by the angular momentum of their dark matter halos, and the latter is determined by the large-scale environment.
galaxies and their components grow with similar angular momentum evolution, and that the angular momentum of stars is conserved on average, with minor fluctuations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the angular momentum of galaxies and their components is not only a function of halo mass, but also depends on the environment and on the sub-grid physics of the simulations.
, despite their differences in the merger history and the sub-grid physics, all the simulated galaxies have a disk-to-halo spin ratio of 0.1–0.2, which is consistent with observations.
the angular momentum evolution is not monotonic, but rather proceeds in bursts, which can be caused either by mergers or secular processes.
